newsitem.title: USA: Satellites line up behind shuttle Columbia.
newsitem.headline: Satellites line up behind shuttle Columbia.

text.p: Shuttle Columbia led a procession of satellites around the globe on Saturday as a prototype space factory and an ultraviolet observatory followed it through space.
The Wake Shield Facility released on Friday night and the Orfeus-Spas orbiting observatory deployed last Tuesday will be retrieved by Columbia's crew later in their 16-day mission.
"That's certainly a beautiful dance out there with three orbiting bodies," spacecraft communicator Bill McArthur told the shuttle crew on Saturday.
It is the first time the shuttle has orbited along with two recoverable satellites and represents a significant challenge for ground controllers, NASA officials said.

"It's a very sophisticated ballet we're doing here," flight director Al Pennington said. "The dynamics of the three-body problem is going to be very tricky. We've spent a lot of time planning for it."

The Wake Shield, a prototype space-based semiconductor factory, had already given the astronauts a scare when it passed close by the shuttle's cockpit minutes after it was released into space on Friday.
The saucer-shaped craft was supposed to have been 24 feet (7.3 metres) from the shuttle but may have come as close as 10 feet (3 metres), shuttle commander Ken Cockrell said.

The astronauts were never in danger because Cockrell could have fired the shuttle's thrusters to take evasive action had a collision looked imminent, NASA officials said. But that would have contaminated the sensitive spacecraft with rocket exhaust, ruining its production of semiconductors.
When the astronauts awoke on Saturday, Columbia was 18 miles (29 km) ahead of the Wake Shield, which was followed 53 miles (85 km) further back by the Orfeus-Spas telescope.
Controllers operating the 2-tonne Wake Shield reported no repeat of the problems with the spacecraft's stabilising system that had caused it to wobble through space during a test flight last year.
"Fortunately ... the Wake Shield is not reeling and rocking," joked mission control's McArthur after waking the crew on Saturday afternoon with a recording of Chuck Berry's "Reeling and Rocking."

The first manufacturing run by the Wake Shield was delayed, however, so controllers could reprogram computers to accommodate several minor technical glitches. The late start will not stop the space factory from growing the seven semiconductor wafers, said Susan Flowers, spokeswoman for Space Industries Inc., which designed the spacecraft with the Space Vacuum Epitaxy Centre at the University of Houston.
"We have room in the schedule. We don't have to be growing every minute to make it," she said.
The Wake Shield creates a pristine vacuum behind a 12-foot (3.7 metre) diameter stainless steel dish in which ultra-pure semiconductors can be manufactured.

If the craft can prove that semiconductors for high-speed computer chips can be manufactured in orbit, it may lead to the first commercial space factory, officials said. Columbia will return on Monday night to pick up the Wake Shield.

Meanwhile, the U.S.-German Orfeus-Spas telescope continued to peer deep into the universe to provide astronomers with new information on the mysterious matter that occupies the space between the stars. The astronauts were to retrieve the orbiting observatory two days before the shuttle's planned Dec. 5 return to Earth.
